newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Gulf Canada battle for Clyde hots up.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Gulf Canada battle for Clyde hots up.

text.p: Gulf Canada Resources Ltd hit out at bid target Clyde Petroleum Plc on Monday, saying the British oil company had used the wrong method and numbers in its defence against Gulf's 432 million pound ($730 million) offer.
"The logic they used is...inappropriate and the methodology is unprecedented," Dick Auchinleck, Gulf Canada's senior vice president of international marketing, told Reuters.
He dismissed the defence Clyde released on Sunday as "thin soup". "There is no meat in this document at all," he said.
While the two firms were locked in a battle over Clyde's value, Clyde shareholders continued to be optimistic of a higher bid emerging either from Gulf or a white knight suitor.
Clyde shares closed 1-1/2 pence higher at 117 pence on Monday, but the premium over Gulf Canada's cash offer of 105p per share did not worry Clyde's advisers.
"It is normal at this stage to see the share price above the offer price," said Nigel Meek of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
But Colin Smith at BZW saw a reasonable chance of a counter bidder emerging at a higher price. "It is unlikely it (Clyde) will go for less than 125 pence," he said.

Auchinleck criticised Clyde for concentrating on its cash flow multiple to defend itself against Gulf Canada's hostile bid, which was launched on December 18. A net asset value (NAV) approach would show that Gulf's offer was fair, he said
"NAV is used unfailingly by every single analyst certainly in this country and it is also the measure North American companies will use to value other companies," Auchinleck said.
"The cash flow multiple itself is a very short-term valuation measure," Auchinleck added.
Clyde reacted quickly, saying it was nonsense to claim net asset valuation was the only method used by British analysts.

Group managing director Roy Franklin said that Clyde's strong cash flow and developing production base made it "directly comparable to our North American peers" which are usually judged on a cash flow basis.
"From the first day of the bid it was clear that what Gulf Canada coveted in Clyde was our strong cash flow," Franklin said.

The net asset value method is used by most British analysts and is based on a company's production from existing oil and gas reserves, ignoring exploration projects which might lead to new production in the future.
Given the long lifetime of oil and gas fields, the net asset value approach has a wider time horizon than the cash flow valuation, which is usually derived from expectations over two to three years.
Analysts using the net asset value method praise its long- term view, allowing for a great variety of adjustable assumptions on such matters as tax and oil prices.
Critics, however, claim too many assumptions have to be made to arrive at any firm conclusions.
Gulf Canada does not want to give its estimate of Clyde's net asset value at this stage and Auchinleck also declined to estimate a fair cash flow multiple for the firm.

In its defence document, Clyde said the bid put it on a cash flow multiple of 5.7 times, comparing unfavourably with similar international companies trading on an historic multiple of 8.9 times or Gulf Canada on 12.7 times.
